paraphrase: In the month of Mārkaḻi, on this good day of the full moon, you girls of the rich cowherd village who will come to bathe, come! Nārāyaṇa himself, the son of Nandagopa, dark-bodied and lotus-eyed, will give us the drum (paṟai).
speaker: Āṇṭāḷ as a cowherd girl
notes: 'mārkaḻit tiṅkaḷ matiniṟainta naṉṉāḷāl ... nārāyaṇaṉē namakkē paṟai taruvāṉ'.

paraphrase: They wake the gatekeeper of Nandagopa's house, then Nandagopa, Yaśodā and Balarāma, then Nappiṉṉai, Kṛṣṇa's beloved, asking her to open the door and bring them to him, and then Kṛṣṇa himself.
speaker: Āṇṭāḷ
notes: Śrīvaiṣṇava commentators read the sequence — gatekeepers (ācāryas), elders, Nappiṉṉai (Śrī as mediator), the Lord — as the order of approach. Verse ranges as recalled.

paraphrase: The observances of the vow: we sing the feet of the Lord who sleeps on the milk ocean; we take no ghee and no milk; we bathe before dawn; we put no kohl on our eyes and no flowers in our hair; we do not do what should not be done; we do not carry evil tales; we give alms and help as much as we can.
speaker: Āṇṭāḷ

paraphrase: We are cowherds who follow the cattle into the forest and eat there, a clan without knowledge; yet we have the merit of your being born among us; the relationship between you and us cannot be broken here even if you try; do not be angry, Govinda, that out of love and ignorance we called you by small names — grant us the drum.
speaker: Āṇṭāḷ
notes: 'uṉtaṉṉōṭu uṟavēl namakku iṅku oḻikka oḻiyātu' — read as the unbreakable relation of soul and Lord and the plea of those with no merit of their own.

paraphrase: We came at dawn to worship your golden lotus feet; hear why: not to take the drum today, Govinda — for all time, for seven times seven births, we shall be kin to you alone and serve you alone; change every other desire of ours.
speaker: Āṇṭāḷ
notes: 'iṟṟaip paṟai koḷvāṉ aṉṟu kāṇ kōvintā ... uṉakkē nām āṭceyvōm maṟṟai nam kāmaṅkaḷ māṟṟu' — the 'drum' is revealed to be service itself.

paraphrase: Those who recite without fail these thirty Tamil verses, sung by Kōtai of Villiputtūr, daughter of Paṭṭarpirāṉ, telling how the cowherd girls obtained the drum, will receive everywhere the grace of the Lord with four shoulders and red eyes, and be happy.
speaker: Āṇṭāḷ

paraphrase: The wondrous one, the son of northern Mathurā, the lamp of the cowherd clan — if we come pure, strew pure flowers, worship him, sing with our mouths and think of him in our minds, then the faults already done and those still to come will burn like cotton in fire; so sing his name.
speaker: Āṇṭāḷ
notes: The threefold worship by body (flowers, bowing), speech (singing) and mind (thinking).

paraphrase: The girls go from house to house at dawn waking their companions — the birds are calling, the conch sounds at the temple, the churning has begun — and chide each sleeper to rise and join the singing of the Lord's names.
speaker: Āṇṭāḷ
notes: Commentators read the awakening of ten companions as seeking the company of devotees before approaching the Lord.
